chunks: And from him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Qunut is in every two rak'ahs in voluntary and obligatory prayers. Al-Hasan said: And Abdullah ibn Bukayr informed me from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): He said: The Qunut is in all prayers.
Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I mentioned that to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said: As for that about which there is no doubt, it is that which is recited aloud.

He (peace be upon him) specifically mentioned in this report and in others from the preceding reports the prayers in which recitation is done aloud, to emphasize the virtue and increase the reward, not to prohibit it in others, as indicated by what we cited of the generality of the phrases, such as their saying (peace be upon them): The Qunut is in all prayers. And like their saying: In every two rak'ahs of the obligatory and voluntary. And also what is narrated from the reports that include the negation of Qunut, such as what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of Qunut in obligatory and voluntary prayers according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia scholarly consensus that Qunut is a recommended act in all prayers, with specific emphasis on those with audible recitation to maximize spiritual reward rather than to restrict the practice. The text resolves apparent contradictions between general and specific reports by interpreting them as complementary rather than exclusive, affirming the permissibility of Qunut even in prayers where it is not explicitly mentioned. This reflects the broader Shia jurisprudential principle of prioritizing voluntary acts of devotion across all prayer types.
